etymologies.etymologyHTML:
From Middle English better, bettre, betre, from Old English betera (“better”), from Proto-West Germanic *batiʀō, from Proto-Germanic *batizô (“better”), from Proto-Indo-European *bʰed-rós, from *bʰed- (“good”).

Cognate with Sanskrit भद्र (bhadrá, “blessed, fortunate, happy, good”) (from *bʰn̥d-ró-s). For Germanic cognates: see Proto-Germanic *batizô. Related to best and battle (“getting better, improving, fruitful, fertile”). Compare also Icelandic batna (“to improve”), bót (“improvement”), German besser. More at batten, boot.

Persian بهتر (behtar) is a false cognate.

quote.text: Badger: You think you're better than other people.Mal: Just the ones I'm better than.
“The air was still with the lonely thrill of 'now the hour is near'  And the smell of sweat was better yet than the awful stench of fear.”

definitions.definition: Greater or lesser (whichever is seen as more advantageous), in reference to value, distance, time, etc.
Healed or recovered from an injury or illness.

quote.citation: c. 1603–1604 (date written), William Shakespeare, “The Tragedie of Othello, the Moore of Venice”, in Mr. William Shakespeares Comedies, Histories, & Tragedies […] (First Folio), London:  […]  Isaac Iaggard, and Ed[ward] Blount, published 1623, →OCLC, [Act I, scene iii]:
quote.text: I could never better stead thee than now. […]

quote.citation: 1901, Louis Couperus, translated by Alexander Teixeira de Mattos, Small Souls:
quote.text: “I’ve had enough of cycling with you chaps. I can spend my Sundays better than in tormenting cats and quarrelling and fighting.”

definitions.definition: An entity, usually animate, deemed superior to another; one who has a claim to precedence; a superior.

quote.citation: 1594–1597, Richard Hooker, edited by J[ohn] S[penser], Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: Their betters would hardly be found.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: From Middle English beteren, from Old English beterian, betrian, from Proto-Germanic *batizōną. Cognate with West Frisian betterje (“to better”), Dutch beteren (“to better”), German bessern (“to better”), Danish bedre (“to better”), Swedish bättra (“to better”).

quote.citation: 1815, William Wordsworth, From the same (To the Supreme Being):
1847 January – 1848 July, William Makepeace Thackeray, chapter 2, in Vanity Fair […], London: Bradbury and Evans […], published 1848, →OCLC:
quote.text: He thought to better his circumstances.

quote.citation: 1849–1861, Thomas Babington Macaulay, chapter III, in The History of England from the Accession of James the Second, volume (please specify |volume=I to V), London: Longman, Brown, Green, and Longmans, →OCLC:
quote.text: the constant effort of every man to better himself

definitions.definition: (transitive) To surpass in excellence; to exceed; to excel.

quote.citation: 1594–1597, Richard Hooker, edited by J[ohn] S[penser], Of the Lawes of Ecclesiastical Politie, […], London:  […]  Will[iam] Stansby [for Matthew Lownes], published 1611, →OCLC, (please specify the page):
quote.text: The works of nature do always aim at that which can not be bettered.

definitions.definition: (transitive) To give advantage to; to support; to advance the interest of.

quote.citation: 1667, John Milton, “Book VI”, in Paradise Lost. […], London:  […]  [Samuel Simmons], and are to be sold by Peter Parker […]; [a]nd by Robert Boulter […]; [a]nd Matthias Walker, […], →OCLC; republished as Paradise Lost in Ten Books: […], London: Basil Montagu Pickering […], 1873, →OCLC:
quote.text: Weapons more violent, when next we meet, / May serve to better us and worse our foes.

etymologies.etymologyHTML: Alternative spelling of bettor or modern formation from the verb to bet +‎ -er.
